draft.title: Reliability and usefulness compared
card: Reliable
A source is reliable when it gives an accurate, trustworthy account of what it describes. Bias, a weak viewpoint or a purpose to persuade can lower reliability.
Useful
A source is useful when it helps answer a particular question. Usefulness depends on the question being asked, not only on whether the source is accurate.
A source can be unreliable for one question yet useful for another. A one-sided recruiting poster is poor evidence of what war was really like.
The same poster is good evidence of how a government wanted people to see the war. Ask what the source can show, then judge it for that question.
draft.remember: Judge a source against the question being asked. One source can be weak for one question and strong for another.

a.q: A recruiting poster shows smiling soldiers and no danger. Why can it still be useful to a historian?
opts: It shows how the government wanted people to see war
It gives an accurate picture of daily life in the trenches
It is reliable because it was made at the time of the war
It is useful because every soldier agreed with its message
a.why: The poster was made to persuade, so it shows the government's message even though it hides the danger. It is not an accurate picture of trench life, and being made at the time does not make a source reliable.
a.clue: Think about what the poster was made to do.

b.q: Liam is asked how a town's council wanted to attract new settlers in the 1880s. He finds a council brochure that exaggerates the town's rich farmland. How should he judge it?
opts: Useful for his question, though unreliable on farmland
Useless, because it exaggerates the quality of the farmland
Reliable, because the council published it officially
Useful only if the farmland claims are all proved true
b.why: His question is about what the council wanted people to believe, and the brochure shows that clearly. Its exaggeration lowers its reliability on the farmland, but that does not make it useless for this question.
b.clue: Match the source to the question, not only to its accuracy.

a.best: It shows how the government wanted people to see war

b.best: Useful for his question, though unreliable on farmland

problems.detail: The distractor 'Useful only if the farmland claims are all proved true' uses 'only', where the card speaks of what a source 'can' show. It is a wrong option, but an absolute word like this can act as a giveaway that it is wrong.

check.summary: The card, remember line, questions and explanations are accurate and match the point; each question has one clearly right answer. The only flag is a minor one: a question b distractor uses 'only', which can tip students off that it is wrong.
